<reason>Both sides built genuinely responsive cases, but CON did more damage to PRO's central pillars. CON's pressure question forced PRO to concede that stripping the "veto over whether and when confirmation happens" is itself a constraint on messaging control — undercutting PRO's separability claim that verification and announcement could stay cleanly decoupled. CON also repeatedly turned the Omicron/South Africa example into a mechanism argument PRO never fully neutralized: mandatory exposure without any power to block retaliation teaches governments to avoid triggering the mechanism at all, meaning forced access risks manufacturing later concealment rather than earlier truth. PRO's best move — using SARS and Wuhan to show sovereign control produces catastrophic delay, and noting sovereignty didn't even protect South Africa from bans — was strong and forced CON into a narrower "discretion over frequency, not immunity" retreat, but PRO's own answers (B4.5, B5.3) mostly asserted that the concealment incentive "isn't new" rather than actually dismantling CON's causal story. CON's closing then directly and cleanly answered PRO's central asymmetry framing ("truth in week one vs. week twelve") with an unanswered rebuttal that forced access guarantees governments never let week one arrive, leaving the decisive comparison on CON's terms.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's pressure question and follow-up (A3.1/A4.1, building on A2.3) forcing PRO to concede that stripping the verification veto is itself the constraint the motion contemplates, directly undercutting PRO's "quiet channel" separability claim.</best_rebuttal>
